rules.Name: User temporary files
rules.Description: What programs write to %TEMP% and are supposed to delete afterwards. Installers and video tools are the usual offenders. Only files untouched for a day are matched, so nothing in use is caught.

rules.Name: Crash dumps
rules.Description: Memory dumps written when a program or the kernel crashed. Useful to whoever is debugging that crash, and to nobody else afterwards.

rules.Name: Error reports queued for Microsoft
rules.Description: Reports Windows collected to send to Microsoft. Removing them means those reports are never sent; nothing on the machine depends on them.

rules.Name: Explorer thumbnail and icon cache
rules.Description: Rebuilt on demand. The first browse through a picture folder afterwards is slower, and that is the entire cost.

rules.Name: DirectX shader cache
rules.Description: Compiled shaders, rebuilt by games and GPU applications as they run. Costs one slower first launch each.

rules.Name: .NET temporary build files
rules.Description: Intermediate files left by ASP.NET and the .NET toolchain. Regenerated on the next build or request.

rules.Name: Chromium browser caches
rules.Description: Chrome, Edge, Opera and Brave page caches. Pages reload from the network afterwards; logins, history and bookmarks are untouched.

rules.Name: Firefox cache
rules.Description: Page and media cache. Reloaded from the network; nothing you are signed into is affected.

rules.Name: NuGet package cache
rules.Description: Downloaded packages, re-fetched on the next restore. On a machine that builds .NET this is often the largest single cache. Needs a network connection to rebuild.

rules.Name: npm cache
rules.Description: Downloaded npm tarballs, re-fetched on the next install. Needs a network connection to rebuild.

rules.Name: pip cache
rules.Description: Downloaded Python wheels, re-fetched on the next install.

rules.Name: Visual Studio Code caches
rules.Description: Editor caches and crash reports. Settings, extensions and workspaces are not touched.

rules.Name: Superseded Windows component store files
rules.Description: Old versions of updated components in WinSxS. Vacuon does not delete these itself — it runs DISM, which is the only supported way and the only one that keeps servicing working. After it runs, the updates it cleaned can no longer be uninstalled.

rules.Name: Turn hibernation off
rules.Description: Frees hiberfil.sys, which is a large fraction of your RAM. This is a configuration change, not a cleanup: hibernate and fast startup stop working until you turn it back on with powercfg /h on.

rules.Name: Old system restore points
rules.Description: Deletes every shadow copy except the most recent one. Those are recovery routes: after this, rolling Windows back to a date before the newest point is no longer possible.
